prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: I moved the optical lattice clock from third to first after reading the openings. It is the one candidate with broad support across very different members: five top-three placements and seven rankings, with Kroll and Lindroth ranking it first and Olsson second. As an instrument builder I judge it on whether it opened a new measurement regime. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts while keeping a large atom number, and the JILA strontium clocks led by Ye took fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18. That is two orders of magnitude beyond what could be done before. The result has been reproduced by several independent groups, so the claim is not in doubt. It supports tests of gravitational redshift and of constants, relativistic geodesy, and the coming redefinition of the second. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori has the concept and first demonstrations, Ye the record accuracy and many-body work. Two names mean a fair pair, with no collaboration-scale cut of the kind that makes the Higgs or EHT hard.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is overlap with earlier metrology prizes (Hall and Hansch 2005 for the comb, Wineland 2012 for ion control). Some of the applied payoff, especially the redefinition of the second, has not yet happened, so recognition could be called early. A third contributor, for example from the Peter Zoller early proposal work or the other clock groups, is outside the credited names and could be argued for. I also have to admit that, as a detector person, I am more comfortable with this kind of result than with condensed-matter or quantum-information candidates, so my confidence in comparing them is lower.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as the clearest case of a measurement technique that changed what can be measured, with Katori's priority clear and Ye taking it to the highest accuracy.
responses.response: I agree with that framing and it is where I have moved. I am less persuaded by his second choice, atom interferometry (B032). The credit there is split across Borde, Pritchard and Kasevich, Chu is missing, and the 1997 laser-cooling prize overlaps. That is a messier attribution than the clock, so I would keep it behind B027 and also behind the aberration-corrected microscope.

responses.point: Eriksson puts topological insulators (B057) first as a clear verified discovery of a new class of quantum matter, with theory by Kane and Mele and the HgTe experiment by Molenkamp.
responses.response: The physics is deep and I take his point that the band-structure prediction was quantitative. My concern is attribution. He himself notes that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe effect that Molenkamp measured, and they are not credited. The 2016 prize on topological phases also reduces the sense of novelty. Since I rely on him and Mehlig for the condensed-matter judgment, I would like to hear whether the HgTe prediction can be separated from the Kane-Mele proposal cleanly enough to defend the three names. Without that, I rank it below the lattice clock.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube's detection of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos first, as a new window on the universe read directly from nature, with Halzen and Karle as a clean pair.
responses.response: This is the field closest to mine and I agree it opened a new window and has been confirmed in several analysis channels, with TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 following. I keep it as an alternative and not first because the discovery paper is a collaboration result and the credited pair reflects leadership of a roughly 300-person project more than a decisive individual contribution. Source identification is also still incomplete. I would be glad to be persuaded otherwise, and this is the candidate I would pair with the clock if the committee wants two parts.

responses.point: Olsson ranks the aberration-corrected electron microscope first as a true instrument breakthrough, with Rose, Haider and Urban fitting the three-way split.
responses.response: I ranked it first in my opening for the same reason, and I still think it is the best example of a tool that broke a limit stated in 1936. I now put it second because of the Krivanek credit problem she names herself, because the committee may see it as materials or chemistry instrumentation, and because it has only two members in support of it. If Eva Lindroth and Stefan Kroll can accept that precedent for instruments, I would be happy to see it as a second part in a later round, but it cannot be combined with the clock without exceeding three people.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as an architecture for strong coupling of an artificial atom to a microwave photon, but notes the overlap with the 2025 prize and the omission of Girvin.
responses.response: I defer to him on the physics. His own two reservations are what concern me: the 2025 prize on circuits was only a year ago, and Girvin and Huard are missing from the credited names. Both make a prize this year hard to defend, and I do not see a reason to put it above the clock.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues treat the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes as a barrier or as a precedent.
Whether the planned redefinition of the second should be completed before the committee rewards the clock.
Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit problem for B057 can be resolved, which would change my ranking of that candidate.
Whether a two-part prize is feasible at all, given the three-person limit and the two-name and three-name candidates.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. None of the credited names in my preferred part are at KTH or in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT or XL-Calibur collaborations. I am a colleague of Eriksson and Johansson on the committee, but that is not a recusal issue.
